commitResults.messageTitle: Rename chatbot from Duke to Bob
Add greeting and farewell messages
Level 1: echouser commands until bye
Level 2: store and list tasks
Level 3: mark tasks as done, add Task class
Level 4: add ToDos, Deadlines and Events with inheritance
commitResults.messageBody:
Add Todo, Deadline and Event subclasses of Task, and make Task abstract
with an abstract getTypeIcon() so every stored task is one of the three
kinds. One Task[] holds any mixture of them, so listing and marking work
unchanged through polymorphism.

Tasks are now added with the todo/deadline/event command words instead of
any bare line, and are confirmed with the task and the running count.
Dates stay as free text, as the requirements allow.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level 5: report input errors by throwing BobException
commitResults.messageBody:
Errors were previously handled by printing a complaint and returning early,
so every command had to know both what a valid command looks like and how the
chatbot prints things. Each unusable command now throws a BobException
carrying the explanation, and one catch in the command loop prints it, putting
the rule "an unusable command is reported, not obeyed" in a single place.

BobException extends Exception rather than RuntimeException so the compiler
insists it is handled: a mistyped command is an expected part of talking to a
chatbot, so it should be impossible to forget. One exception class is enough
while the response to every error is the same; subclasses would be the next
step if catch ever needed to tell them apart.

Three behaviours change for the user:

- mark and unmark now match the command word on its own, so a bare "mark" is
  answered with "which task?" instead of "I don't know what that means".
- A blank line gets its own prompt rather than being quoted back as unknown.
- mark on an empty list says the list is empty instead of quoting a range of
  task numbers that does not exist.

Messages name the specific missing piece — a deadline can fail four different
ways — and pair the diagnosis with a working example.

Test plan: TC5 and TC7 revised for the new wording; TC9 covers the remaining
malformed add commands, TC10 blank lines, and TC11 interleaves valid and
invalid commands to check that a refused command stores and marks nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Level 6: delete tasks, and store them in an ArrayList
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a 'delete <task number>' command that removes a task and confirms it by showing the task itself. Deleting renumbers every task below it, so the number the user typed no longer refers to the same task afterwards; showing the task is what confirms the right one went.

Switch the task store from a fixed Task[100] plus a manual taskCount to an ArrayList<Task> (extension A-Collections). Deletion on an array would mean shifting later elements down by hand and keeping the count in step with the contents; the list does both itself, and size() becomes the single source of truth for how many tasks there are. This also removes the 100-task cap and its 'list is full' error, which no longer has a case to report.

Factor the task-number checking shared by mark, unmark and delete into requireTaskIndex, so the four ways a task number can be wrong are rejected in one place instead of three.

Update the UI test plan: TC5 and TC9 now expect delete among the known commands, and TC12-TC15 cover deletion from the middle and the ends of the list, its error cases, emptying the list, and marking after a deletion following the new numbering.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Enums: replace the command-word constants with a Command enum
commitResults.messageBody:
Move the eight command words out of Bob into a Command enum. They are a fixed set known at compile time, so an enum lets the compiler know the whole set: a command travels as a Command rather than as a String that could hold any text, and requireTaskIndex can no longer be handed a command word that does not exist.

Two duplications go away. The list of commands offered after an unrecognised line is now built from values() instead of being spelled out by hand, so it cannot fall out of step with the commands that exist - it had to be updated separately when delete was added in Level 6. And the if-else chain in handleCommand becomes a switch over the enum, one branch per constant.

Give each constant a takesArguments flag. This states a rule that was previously implicit in which branch of the chain a command sat in: list and bye match only their exact keyword, while the other six also match the keyword followed by arguments. That is what keeps 'bye now' from ending the conversation and 'list foo' from listing.

Behaviour is unchanged: all 15 existing test cases pass without their expected output being touched, and the pre- and post-refactor programs produce byte-identical output on a set of awkward inputs. Add TC16 to guard the argument-less commands, which nothing in the plan covered.

commitResults.messageTitle: UI test plan: Cover dates the chatbot understands
Add on, before and next commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadlines and events hold their dates as understood dates rather than copied text, but nothing is ever asked of them. Finding what is due on a day gets tedious as the  list grows long.

Let's add three views of the task list:
* on <date>, the tasks falling on that day
* before <date>, the tasks falling earlier than that day
* next <how many>, the tasks with the soonest dates, most urgent first

commitResults.messageTitle: UI test plan: Cover asking about dates
Add after command
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot can be asked what falls on a day and what falls before one,
but not what falls after one. The obvious third question is left
unanswerable: someone who wants to know what is still to come past a
date has to read the whole list and work it out.

Let's add an after command alongside on and before. It takes a day
written the same way those two do, and lists the dated tasks pinned to
a later day, numbered as they are in list so a task found this way can
be marked or deleted straight away.

A task is placed by the single date it is pinned to, which for an event
is its start. An event running across the day asked about is therefore
not listed as still to come, and on is the command that finds that one.
Placing an event by its end instead would leave after and before
disagreeing about where the same event sits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject an event that ends before it starts
commitResults.messageBody:
An event's start and its end are each checked to be a readable date,
but nothing checks them against each other. A pair typed the wrong way
round, such as /from 2026-12-05 /to 2026-12-02, is stored as written,
and the event then sits in the list claiming to run backwards.

Let's refuse such a pair when the event is added, and quote both dates
back in the complaint so the user can see which one was read as the
start and which as the end.

The check belongs in the command rather than in Event, because the
command is where there is still a user to tell about it. An event read
from a hand-edited save file therefore goes unchecked, which is the one route into Event that does not pass through the command.

A start and an end at the same moment are accepted. That is a point in
time rather than a contradiction, and someone who means it should be
able to say so.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
Extract user interaction into a Ui class
commitResults.messageBody:
Bob decides what each command does and also controls how every line of
the answer reaches the screen. It holds the indent, the rules that
frame a block of output, the startup banner and the greeting, and it is
the only class that touches System.out and System.in.

Holding both concerns makes each harder to change. Altering how the
chatbot looks means editing the class that decides what its commands
mean, and every command has to know the printing convention rather than
simply saying what it wants said.

Let's move the conversation into a new Ui class: the banner and the
greeting, the farewell, the rules that open and close a block, the
printing of an error message, and the reading of the user's input. Bob
keeps one Ui and hands it lines of plain text.

Reading input goes with printing rather than staying behind, because it
is the other half of the same conversation. No other class now needs to
know that the user's typing arrives on System.in through a Scanner.

This is the first step towards splitting Bob into the four classes the
increment asks for, so it moves the display code alone and leaves the
task list and the command parsing where they are. Nothing the user sees
changes, and all 29 text UI test cases still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract the task list into a TaskList class
commitResults.messageBody:
Bob keeps its tasks in a bare ArrayList field and reaches into it from
nine places. Every command therefore knows how the tasks are stored: how
to walk the list, that it counts from 0 while the user counts from 1,
and how to search it. Two of the listing commands carry a loop over the
list of their own, written out where the printing is.

That spreads one decision across the whole class. It also leaves no
place to put an operation on the list as a whole, so the searching that
on, before, after and next need has to live beside the code that prints
their answers, mixing what is being looked for with how it is shown.

Let's give the tasks a class of their own, holding the list and the
operations performed on it: add, delete, get, size, a search by any test
a caller cares to pass, and the ordering of the dated tasks by how soon
they fall due. Bob keeps a TaskList and no longer knows the tasks sit in
a list at all.

The two searches return positions in the list rather than the tasks
found. The user names a task by the number it has in list, so a
shortened listing is only useful if it shows each task under that same
number; a number counting the matches could not be typed into mark or
delete afterwards.

Validation stays in Bob. A task number that names no task is a mistake
made by a user who is still there to be told about it, whereas TaskList
has only a position and no way to explain anything, so it assumes the
position exists exactly as a plain list does.

Storage still takes a plain List<Task>, supplied by asList(), because
writing tasks to a file needs nothing more than walking them in order.
Asking for less is what keeps the two classes apart.

Nothing the user sees changes, and all 29 text UI test cases still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command parsing into a Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
Every command in Bob begins by picking its own arguments apart. Adding a
deadline is one method that finds /by, complains about the three ways the
text around it can be wrong, reads the date, and only then builds the
task and stores it. Seven of the eight constants in the class exist only
to be quoted back in those complaints.

Two jobs are being done in each of those methods: working out what the
user asked for, and carrying it out. Because they are written together,
the rules for how a command may be typed are scattered over the class
rather than stated anywhere, and there is no one place to look when
changing what the chatbot accepts.

Let's move the reading of a line into a class of its own. Parser is given
the text and hands back the thing meant by it: a Todo, a Deadline, an
Event, a task number, a day, or a count. Bob is left with methods that
are given a finished value and get on with using it, and the three add
commands collapse into one line apiece.

Parser makes sense of text and of nothing else. Whether the number 7
names a task that exists is a fact about the list rather than about what
was typed, so that check stays in Bob, which is the class holding the
list. The line is worth drawing because both refusals read alike to the
user: mark seven is refused by the parser, mark 7 with four tasks by Bob.

Its methods are static, unlike Ui, Storage and TaskList, which are made
and kept. A parser has nothing to remember between one line and the
next, so an instance would carry no state and be no more useful than the
class itself.

The three separate example constants for on, before and after are
replaced by one method that builds the example from the command word.
They were the same formula written out three times, which is three
chances to forget one when a fourth such command is added.

Nothing the user sees changes, and all 29 text UI test cases still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Bob an object rather than a class of statics
commitResults.messageBody:
Bob is made entirely of static fields and static methods. It works with
three things that have state of their own, a Ui, a Storage and a
TaskList, but holds them as class variables, so there can only ever be
one chatbot and it can only ever read the one hard-coded save file.

Two costs follow. The task list cannot be final: a static field cannot
be set by a constructor, so it starts as an empty placeholder and is
replaced once the save file has been read, leaving a window in which the
field holds something that is not the answer. And the class cannot be
tested, because there is no way to make one pointed at a scratch file
instead of at the user's own tasks.

Let's give the class a constructor that takes the file to use, builds the
three collaborators, and reads the saved tasks, and a run method that
holds the conversation. Every field becomes final and the compiler
enforces it. Only main stays static, since it is called before there is
an object to call it on; it makes one and steps aside.

The tasks are read in the constructor but the report on reading them is
not printed there. The greeting has to come first, and a constructor
that printed would be deciding when its own output appeared, so the
messages Storage returns are held in a field and printed by run once the
greeting is out.

This completes the split the increment asks for: Ui, Storage, Parser and
TaskList, with Bob left saying what each command does. Nothing the user
sees changes, and all 29 text UI test cases still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename the Command enum to CommandWord
commitResults.messageBody:
The enum named Command holds the words the chatbot accepts at the start
of a line, and the rules for recognizing one: the keyword, whether
anything may follow it, and the lookup that turns a line into a
constant. It says nothing about what is to be done once a word has been
recognized, which is decided by a switch in Bob.

The next step is to give each command a class that knows how to carry
itself out, and the natural name for those is Command. The name is
taken, by a type that describes only the vocabulary.

Let's rename the enum to CommandWord, which is what it has always been
about, and leave the plainer name free. Nothing else changes: the enum
keeps every constant and every method it had, and this commit is a
rename and its 75 call sites.

Keeping both types, rather than folding the enum into the new classes,
is deliberate. Recognizing which word a line starts with is a question
about text that is worth answering in one table, while what each command
does is behaviour that is worth answering with a method. Merging them
would put the vocabulary back into the same place as the doing.

Nothing the user sees changes, and all 29 text UI test cases still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ui: take over how tasks are shown
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui frames the output but does not compose it. The fixed wording of every
confirmation, and the numbering of a listing, are written out by whoever
runs the command. Four commands produce a listing, and each carries its
own loop over the positions and its own copy of the rule that the user
counts from 1 while the list counts from 0.

Giving each command a class of its own is the next step, and on this
footing every one of those classes would carry a few lines of layout
that are the same in all of them. Wording that never varies belongs to
the class whose subject is what the chatbot says.

Let's move the listing and the confirmations into Ui. It gains a method
that prints a numbered selection of tasks, one for each of the three
confirmations, and the report on what was loaded from the save file. The
wording that varies with the command is still passed in, since only the
command knows the day it looked at or how many urgent tasks it found.

The shared helper in Bob that walked a listing is gone, and the four
listing commands are now three or four lines each that say what they
looked for and what to call it.

This makes Ui depend on Task and TaskList, which is the right way round:
what shows the tasks may know what a task is, while a task knows nothing
about being shown.

TaskList gains allIndexes, so that a full listing is produced the same
way as a shortened one and both are shown by the same code.

Nothing the user sees changes, and all 29 text UI test cases still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give each command a class of its own
commitResults.messageBody:
Bob decides what every command does. A switch names all twelve of them
and sends each to a method beside it, so the whole of the chatbot's
behavior sits in the one class that also runs the conversation. Adding a
command means editing Bob in three places: a branch, a method, and
whatever the method needs.

Let's make each command a class with an execute method, under an
abstract Command that says every command can be carried out and can be
asked whether it was the last one. Parser stops returning a word and its
arguments and returns the command itself, ready to run.

The loop in run no longer asks which command it is holding. It parses a
line, runs what comes back, and asks whether that was the end. A command
can now be added to the chatbot without run changing at all.

Two commands share a parent below Command. Mark and delete both name a
task by its number and both have to check that the list holds one, which
Parser cannot do because it reads text and has no list to count. Sharing
the check is worth a class; sharing the shape is not, which is why on,
before and after stay three plain classes rather than three subclasses of
a fourth that would leave each too thin to read.

The switch that named every command is not gone but changed in kind. It
now turns a word into an object, which something has to do somewhere,
and no longer says what any of them does.

Parser keeps one public method. The halfway houses it used to expose — a
date read out of some text, a task number, a description — are steps on
the way to a command and not answers anyone outside wants.

TC30 covers input that ends without bye, which no test case reached
before. The farewell is now printed by the bye command, so a run whose
input simply stops has to be given one separately, and that path was the
one thing here that could have broken unnoticed.

Nothing the user sees changes, and all 30 text UI test cases pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreOOP'
Organize classes into packages
commitResults.messageBody:
All 23 classes sit in one bob package, so nothing in the ource
tree says which of them is the model, which talks to the console, and
which reads the save file.

A flat package also hides coupling: any class can reach any other with
no import to show for it, so a dependency that should not exist looks
exactly like one that should.

Let's group the classes by the job they do ( bob.task, bob.command,
bob.parser, bob.storage and bob.ui) keeping src/main/java as the
source root.

Bob and BobException stay in the root package.

CommandWord moves in with the commands rather than the parser. Both use
it, but the commands use it in their own code, so leaving it beside
Parser would leave bob.command and bob.parser importing each other. The
resulting package graph is acyclic, with bob.task at the bottom.

Add find command to search task descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot can be asked what falls on a day, before one, or after
one, but never about the words in a task. Someone who remembers a task
only by a word in its description has no way to pick it out but to
read the whole list.

Let's add a find command that lists the tasks whose description
mentions a keyword, under the numbers those tasks have in list, so one
found this way can be marked or deleted without looking it up again.

The search ignores case and matches part of a word. A user reaching
for a task cannot be expected to remember how they capitalized it, and
half a word is a search someone types on purpose.

Deciding what counts as a match is left to Task, so the command only
asks the question, exactly as the three date listings already do.
Unlike them, this one finds a todo too: every task has a description,
even the ones with no date.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JavaDoc'
Merge branch 'branch-A-CodingStandard'
Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
Let the chatbot answer without printing
commitResults.messageBody:
Everything the chatbot says goes straight to System.out, and the only
way to ask it anything is to let it read a line from the keyboard
itself. A front end that is not a console has neither: it must hand
over a line it already has, and be given the answer back as text to
place on screen itself.

Let's give Ui two shapes, one printing and one collecting, and give
Bob the three methods a windowed front end holds a conversation
through: getGreeting, getResponse and isExit.

Both front ends run their commands through one new method, so neither
can drift into answering differently from the other. What the console
prints is unchanged, which the text UI test plan confirms.

Ui keeps to one class rather than gaining a subclass per front end,
because the two differ only in where a finished line goes, and not in
what is said or in what order.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a JavaFX window as a second front end
commitResults.messageBody:
Bob can only be used from a console, which means being comfortable
with a terminal and with a program that owns it until you type bye. A
window is what most users expect of a chat program, and the chatbot
can now supply one: its answers already come back as text.

Let's add a JavaFX front end showing the conversation as speech
bubbles, and point Gradle's run task and the packaged jar at it. The
console front end is untouched, and is still what the text UI test
plan runs.

The window's arrangement lives in FXML and its colors in CSS rather
than in Java, so the part most often changed by eye can be changed
without recompiling anything. Launcher exists only to call
Application.launch from a class that does not extend Application,
which is what lets the jar start where JavaFX sits on the class path.

JavaFX is not added as a dependency: the JDK this project builds on
carries it already, so the org.openjfx jars would only put a second
copy on the class path for the JDK's own modules to shadow.
